entries.7141adc15b0d7693476b100a07ad08e8c5e075cb: <div sID="gen9069" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Esth.7" sID="Esth.7"/> <div eID="gen9069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9070" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9071" type="x-p"/> We are now to attend the second banquet to which the king and Haman were invited: and there, I. Esther presents her petition to the king for her life and the life of her people, <reference osisRef="Esth.7.1-Esth.7.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. She plainly tells the king that Haman is the man who designed her ruin and the ruin of all her friends, <reference osisRef="Esth.7.5-Esth.7.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>. III. The king thereupon gave orders for the hanging of Haman upon the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai, which was done accordingly, <reference osisRef="Esth.7.7-Esth.7.10">ver. 7-10</reference>. And thus, by the destruction of the plotter, a good step was taken towards the defeating of the plot.
entries.9a1a7c417099806a394fa7847f1e7b94e96c7750: <div eID="gen9071" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9070" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Haman Accused by Esther. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 510.)</title> <div sID="gen9072" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> So the king and Haman came to banquet with Esther the queen. <hi type="super">2</hi> And the king said again unto Esther on the second day at the banquet of wine, What <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy petition, queen Esther? and it shall be granted thee: and what <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy request? and it shall be performed, <hi type="italic">even</hi> to the half of the kingdom. <hi type="super">3</hi> Then Esther the queen answered and said, If I have found favour in thy sight, O king, and if it please the king, let my life be given me at my petition, and my people at my request: <hi type="super">4</hi> For we are sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be slain, and to perish. But if we had been sold for bondmen and bondwomen, I had held my tongue, although the enemy could not countervail the king's damage. <hi type="super">5</hi> Then the king Ahasuerus answered and said unto Esther the queen, Who is he, and where is he, that durst presume in his heart to do so? <hi type="super">6</hi> And Esther said, The adversary and enemy <hi type="italic">is</hi> this wicked Haman. Then Haman was afraid before the king and the queen. <div eID="gen9072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9073" type="x-p"/> The king in humour, and Haman out of humour, meet at Esther's table. Now, <div eID="gen9073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9074" type="x-p"/> I. The king urged Esther, a third time, to tell him what her request was, for he longed to know, and repeated his promise that it should be granted, <reference osisRef="Esth.7.2">v. 2</reference>. If the king had now forgotten that Esther had an errand to him, and had not again asked what it was, she could scarcely have known how to renew it herself; but he was mindful of it, and now was bound with the threefold cord of a promise thrice made to favour her. <div eID="gen9074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9075" type="x-p"/> II. Esther, at length, surprises the king with a petition, not for wealth or honour, or the preferment of some of her friends to some high post, which the king expected, but for the preservation of herself and her countrymen from death and destruction, <reference osisRef="Esth.7.3-Esth.7.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. <div eID="gen9075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9076" type="x-p"/> 1. Even a stranger, a criminal, shall be permitted to petition for his life; but that a friend, a wife, should have occasion to present such a petition was very affecting: <hi type="italic">Let my life be given me at my petition, and my people at my request.</hi> Two things bespeak lives to be very precious, and fit to be saved, if innocent, at any expense:—(1.) Majesty. If it be a crowned head that is struck at, it is time to stir. Esther's was such: "<hi type="italic">Let my life be given me.</hi> If thou hast any affection for the wife of thy bosom, now is the time to show it; for that is the life that lies at stake." (2.) Multitude. If they be many lives, very many, and those no way forfeited, that are aimed at, no time should be lost nor pains spared to prevent the mischief. "It is not a friend or two, but <hi type="italic">my people,</hi> a whole nation, and a nation dear to me, for the saving of which I now intercede." <div eID="gen9076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9077" type="x-p"/> 2. To move the king the more she suggests, (1.) That she and her people were bought and sold. They had not sold themselves by any offence against the government, but were sold to gratify the pride and revenge of one man. (2.) That it was not their liberty only, but their lives that were sold. "Had we been sold" (she says) "into slavery, I would not have complained; for in time we might have recovered our liberty, thought the king would have made but a bad bargain of it, and not have increased his wealth by our price. Whatever had been paid for us, the loss of so many industrious hands out of his kingdom would have been more damage to the treasury than the price would countervail." To persecute good people is as impolitic as it is impious, and a manifest wrong to the interests of princes and states; they are weakened and impoverished by it. But this was not the case. <hi type="italic">We are sold</hi> (says she) <hi type="italic">to be destroyed, to be slain, and to perish;</hi> and then it is time to speak. She refers to the words of the decree (<reference osisRef="Esth.3.13">ch. iii. 13</reference>), which aimed at nothing short of their destruction; this would touch in a tender part if there were any such in the king's heart, and would bring him to relent. <div eID="gen9077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9078" type="x-p"/> III. The king stands amazed at the remonstrance, and asks (<reference osisRef="Esth.7.5">v. 5</reference>) "<hi type="italic">Who is he, and where is he, that durst presume in his heart to do so?</hi> What! contrive the murder of the queen and all her friends? Is there such a man, such a monster rather, in nature? <hi type="italic">Who is he, and where is he, whose heart has filled him to do so?</hi>" Or, Who hath <hi type="italic">filled his heart.</hi> He wonders, 1. That any one should be so bad as to think such a thing; Satan certainly filled his heart. 2. That any one should be so bold as to do such a thing, should have his heart so fully set in him to do wickedly, should be so very daring. Note, (1.) It is hard to imagine that there should be such horrid wickedness committed in the world as really there is. Who, where is he, that dares, presumes, to question the being of God and his providence, to banter his oracles, profane his name, persecute his people, and yet bid defiance to his wrath? Such there are, to think of whom is enough to make <hi type="italic">horror take hold of us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.119.53">Ps. cxix. 53</reference>. (2.) We sometimes startle at the mention of that evil which yet we ourselves are chargeable with. Ahasuerus is amazed at that wickedness which he himself is guilty of; for he consented to that bloody edict against the Jews. <hi type="italic">Thou art the man,</hi> might Esther too truly have said. <div eID="gen9078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9079" type="x-p"/> IV. Esther plainly charged Haman with it before his face: "Here he is, let him speak for himself, for therefore he is invited: <hi type="italic">The adversary and enemy is this wicked Haman</hi> (<reference osisRef="Esth.7.6">v. 6</reference>); it is he that has designed our murder, and, which is worse, has basely drawn the king in to be <hi type="italic">particeps criminis—a partaker of his crime,</hi> ignorantly agreeing to it." <div eID="gen9079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9080" type="x-p"/> V. Haman is soon apprehensive of his danger: <hi type="italic">He was afraid before the king and queen;</hi> and it was time for him to fear when the queen was his prosecutor, the king his judge, and his own conscience a witness against him; and the surprising operations of Providence against him that same morning could not but increase his fear. Now he has little joy of his being invited to the banquet of wine, but finds himself in straits when he thought himself <hi type="italic">in the fulness of his sufficiency. He is cast into a net by his own feet.</hi>
entries.2c586dd936d90d849e6e3ceaa309a1254b5e00c1: <div eID="gen9080" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The King Incensed Against Haman; Haman Hanged upon His Own Gallows. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  510.)</title> <div sID="gen9081" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> And the king arising from the banquet of wine in his wrath <hi type="italic">went</hi> into the palace garden: and Haman stood up to make request for his life to Esther the queen; for he saw that there was evil determined against him by the king. <hi type="super">8</hi> Then the king returned out of the palace garden into the place of the banquet of wine; and Haman was fallen upon the bed whereon Esther <hi type="italic">was.</hi> Then said the king, Will he force the queen also before me in the house? As the word went out of the king's mouth, they covered Haman's face. <hi type="super">9</hi> And Harbonah, one of the chamberlains, said before the king, Behold also, the gallows fifty cubits high, which Haman had made for Mordecai, who had spoken good for the king, standeth in the house of Haman. Then the king said, Hang him thereon. <hi type="super">10</hi> So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then was the king's wrath pacified. <div eID="gen9081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9082" type="x-p"/> Here, I. The king retires in anger. He rose from table in a great passion, and <hi type="italic">went into the palace garden</hi> to cool himself and to consider what was to be done, <reference osisRef="Esth.7.7">v. 7</reference>. He sent not for his <hi type="italic">seven wise counsellors who knew the times,</hi> being ashamed to consult them about the undoing of that which he had rashly done without their knowledge or advice; but he went to walk in the garden awhile, to compare in his thoughts what Esther had now informed him of with what had formerly passed between him and Haman. And we may suppose him, 1. Vexed at himself, that he should be such a fool as to doom a guiltless nation to destruction, and his own queen among the rest, upon the base suggestions of a self-seeking man, without examining the truth of his allegations. Those that do things with self-will reflect upon them afterwards with self-reproach. 2. Vexed at Haman whom he had laid in his bosom, that he should be such a villain as to abuse his interest in him to draw him to consent to so wicked a measure. When he saw himself betrayed by one he had caressed he was full of indignation at him; yet he would say nothing till he had taken time for second thoughts, to see whether they would make the matter better or worse than it first appeared, that he might proceed accordingly. When we are angry we should pause awhile before we come to any resolution, as those that have <hi type="italic">a rule over our own spirits</hi> and are governed by reason. <div eID="gen9082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9083" type="x-p"/> II. Haman becomes a humble petitioner to the queen for his life. He might easily perceived by the king's hastily flying out of the room that <hi type="italic">there was evil determined against him.</hi> For <hi type="italic">the wrath of a king,</hi> such a king, <hi type="italic">is as the roaring of a lion</hi> and as <hi type="italic">messengers of death;</hi> and now see, 1. How mean Haman looks, when he stands up first and then falls down at Esther's feet, to beg she would save his life and take all he had. Those that are most haughty, insolent, and imperious, when they are in power and prosperity, are commonly the most abject and poor-spirited when the wheel turns upon them. Cowards, they say, are most cruel, and then consciousness of their cruelty makes them the more cowardly. 2. How great Esther looks, who of late had been neglected and doomed to the slaughter <hi type="italic">tanquam ovis—as a sheep;</hi> now her sworn enemy owns that he lies at her mercy, and begs his life at her hand. Thus did God <hi type="italic">regard the low estate of his handmaiden</hi> and <hi type="italic">scatter the proud in the imagination of their hearts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.48">Luke i. 48</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.51">51</reference>. Compare with this that promise made to the Philadelphian church (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.9">Rev. iii. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will make those of the synagogue of Satan to come and to worship before thy feet and to know that I have loved thee.</hi> The day is coming when those that hate and persecute God's chosen ones would gladly be beholden to them. <hi type="italic">Give us of your oil. Father Abraham, send Lazarus. The upright shall have dominion in the morning.</hi> <div eID="gen9083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9084" type="x-p"/> III. The king returns yet more exasperated against Haman. The more he thinks of him the worse he thinks of him and of what he had done. It was but lately that every thing Haman said and did, even that which was most criminal, was taken well and construed to his advantage; now, on the contrary, what Haman did that was not only innocent, but a sign of repentance, is ill taken, and, without colour of reason, construed to his disadvantage. He lay in terror at Esther's feet, to beg for his life. What! (says the king) <hi type="italic">will he force the queen also before me in the house?</hi> Not that he thought he had any such intention, but having been musing on Haman's design to slay the queen, and finding him in this posture, he takes occasion from it thus to vent his passion against Haman, as a man that would not scruple at the greatest and most impudent piece of wickedness. "He designed to slay the queen, and to slay her <hi type="italic">wish me in the house;</hi> will he in like manner force her? What! ravish her first and then murder her? He that had a design upon her life may well be suspected to have a design upon her chastity." <div eID="gen9084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9085" type="x-p"/> IV. Those about him were ready to be the instruments of his wrath. The courtiers that adored Haman when he was the rising sun set themselves as much against him now that he is a falling star, and are even glad of an occasion to run him down: so little sure can proud men be of the interest they think they have. 1. As soon as the king spoke an angry word <hi type="italic">they covered Haman's face,</hi> as a condemned man, not worthy any more either to see the king or to be seen by him; they marked him for execution. Those that are hanged commonly have their faces covered. See how ready the servants were to take the first hint of the king's mind in this matter. <hi type="italic">Turba Romae sequitur fortunam, et semper et odit damnatos—The Roman populace change as the aspects of fortune do, and always oppress the fallen.</hi> If Haman be going down, they all cry, "Down with him." 2. One of those that had been lately sent to Haman's house, to fetch him to the banquet, informed the king of the gallows which Haman had prepared for Mordecai, <reference osisRef="Esth.7.9">v. 9</reference>. Now that Mordecai is the favourite the chamberlain applauds him—he <hi type="italic">spoke good for the king;</hi> and, Haman being in disgrace, every thing is taken notice of that might make against him, incense the king against him, and fill up the measure of his iniquity. <div eID="gen9085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9086" type="x-p"/> V. The king gave orders that he should be hanged upon his own gallows, which was done accordingly, nor was he so much as asked what he had to say why this judgment should not be passed upon him and execution awarded. The sentence is short—<hi type="italic">Hang him thereon;</hi> and the execution speedy—<hi type="italic">So they hanged Haman on the gallows,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.7.10">v. 10</reference>. See here, 1. Pride brought down. He that expected every one to do him homage is now made an ignominious spectacle to the world, and he himself sacrificed to his revenge. God resists the proud; and those whom he resists will find him irresistible. 2. Persecution punished. Haman was upon many accounts a wicked man, but his enmity to God's church was his most provoking crime, and for <hi type="italic">that</hi> the God to whom vengeance belongs here reckons with him, and, though his plot was defeated, gives him <hi type="italic">according to the wickedness of his endeavours,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.28.4">Ps. xxviii. 4</reference>. 3. Mischief returned upon the person himself that contrived it, the <hi type="italic">wicked snared in the work of his own hands,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.7.15-Ps.7.16">Ps. vii. 15, 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.9.15-Ps.9.16">ix. 15, 16</reference>. Haman was justly hanged on the very gallows he had unjustly prepared for Mordecai. If he had not set up that gallows, perhaps the king would not have thought of ordering him to be hanged; but, if he rear a gallows for <hi type="italic">the man whom the king delights to honour,</hi> the thought is very natural that he should be ordered to try it himself, and see how it fits him, see how he likes it. The enemies of God's church have often been thus taken in their own craftiness. In the morning Haman was designing himself for the robes and Mordecai for the gallows; but the tables are turned: Mordecai has the crown, Haman the cross. <hi type="italic">The Lord is known by such judgments.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Prov.11.8">Prov. xi. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.21.18">xxi. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen9086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9087" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> The satisfaction which the king had in this execution. <hi type="italic">Then was the king's wrath pacified,</hi> and not till then. He was as well pleased in ordering Haman to be hanged as in ordering Mordecai to be honoured. Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delights to take vengeance on. God saith of wicked men (<reference osisRef="Ezek.5.13">Ezek. v. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will cause my fury to rest upon them, and I will be comforted.</hi>  <chapter eID="Esth.7"/> <div eID="gen9087" type="x-p"/>

entries.0b06cdcdafb393801e4a32989b6d088a883a3417: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4436"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 7</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Esth.7.1-Esth.7.6">Es 7:1-6</reference>. Esther Pleads for Her Own Life and the Life of Her People.</title> <div sID="gen6415" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4436"/><hi type="bold">4. we are sold, I and my people, to be destroyed--</hi>that is, by the cruel and perfidious scheme of that man, who offered an immense sum of money to purchase our extermination. Esther dwelt on his contemplated atrocity, in a variety of expressions, which both evinced the depth of her own emotions, and were intended to awaken similar feelings in the king's breast.<div eID="gen6415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6416" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">But if we had been sold for bondmen and bondwomen, I had held my tongue--</hi>Though a great calamity to the Jews, the enslavement of that people might have enriched the national treasury; and, at all events, the policy, if found from experience to be bad, could be altered. But the destruction of such a body of people would be an irreparable evil, and all the talents Haman might pour into the treasury could not compensate for the loss of their services. <div eID="gen6416" type="x-p"/>
entries.84cafaa83ee86e7cd3b299f2d2b0ad11f6067958: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4437"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Esth.7.7-Esth.7.10">Es 7:7-10</reference>. The King Causes Haman to Be Hanged on His Own Gallows.</title> <div sID="gen6417" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4437"/><hi type="bold">7. he saw that there was evil determined against him by the king--</hi>When the king of Persia orders an offender to be executed, and then rises and goes into the women's apartment, it is a sign that no mercy is to be hoped for. Even the sudden rising of the king in anger was the same as if he had pronounced sentence. <div eID="gen6417" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe56ee9d7b3002b1e4c8cb6f03f0ac74c6b8c589: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4438"/><div sID="gen6418" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4438"/><hi type="bold">8. Haman was fallen upon the bed whereon Esther was--</hi>We do not know the precise form of the couches on which the Persians reclined at table. But it is probable that they were not very different from those used by the Greeks and Romans. Haman, perhaps, at first stood up to beg pardon of Esther; but driven in his extremity to resort to an attitude of the most earnest supplication, he fell prostrate on the couch where the queen was recumbent. The king returning that instant was fired at what seemed an outrage on female modesty.<div eID="gen6418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6419" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they covered Haman's face--</hi>The import of this striking action is, that a criminal is unworthy any longer to look on the face of the king, and hence, when malefactors are consigned to their doom in Persia, the first thing is to cover the face with a veil or napkin. <div eID="gen6419" type="x-p"/>
entries.dfb0b16b5ab6c5a366de449c5f28281046767dc3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4439"/><div sID="gen6420" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4439"/><hi type="bold">9. Harbonah, one of the chamberlains, said before the king, Behold also, the gallows--</hi>This eunuch had probably been the messenger sent with the invitation to Haman, and on that occasion had seen the gallows. The information he now volunteered, as well it may be from abhorrence of Haman's cold-blooded conspiracy as from sympathy with his amiable mistress, involved with her people in imminent peril. <div eID="gen6420" type="x-p"/>
entries.20522dc0e2e95215741036d685c520d7ccdb084f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4440"/><div sID="gen6421" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4440"/><hi type="bold">10. So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai--</hi>He has not been the only plotter of mischief whose feet have been taken in the net which they hid (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.15">Psa 9:15</reference>). But never was condemnation more just, and retribution more merited, than the execution of that gigantic criminal. <chapter eID="Esth.7"/>

entries.a5e3fabc6ed517afe58fd660f2fb6e5576951de0: <div eID="gen15576" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen15577" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15578" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15578" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15577" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15579" type="x-p"/> The king at the banquet urges Esther to prefer her petition, with the positive assurance that it shall be granted, <reference osisRef="Est.7.1">Est 7:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Est.7.2">Est 7:2</reference>. She petitions for her own life, and the life of her people, who were sold to be destroyed, <reference osisRef="Est.7.3">Est 7:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Est.7.4">Est 7:4</reference>. The king inquires the author of this project, and Haman is accused by the queen, <reference osisRef="Est.7.5">Est 7:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Est.7.6">Est 7:6</reference>. The king is enraged: Haman supplicates for his life; but the king orders him to be hanged on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai, <reference osisRef="Est.7.7-Est.7.10">Est 7:7-10</reference>.
entries.307012282040fbfa578662e37458d1a5e0db9c1d: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen15579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15580" type="x-p"/> At the banquet of wine - Postquam vino incaluerat, after he had been heated with wine, says the Vulgate. In such a state the king was more likely to come into the measures of the queen.
entries.c6a4652d72f3345b81344399cf1b6a3bc6df9cb8: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen15580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15581" type="x-p"/> Let my life be given me - This was very artfully, as well as very honestly, managed; and was highly calculated to work on the feelings of the king. What! is the life of the queen, whom I most tenderly love, in any kind of danger?
entries.bb29aab9679511c6fd875a579a360c7f4d31460d: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen15581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15582" type="x-p"/> To be destroyed, to be slain - She here repeats the words which Haman put into the decree. See <reference osisRef="Est.3.13">Est 3:13</reference>. <div eID="gen15582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15583" type="x-p"/> Could not countervail the king's damage - Even the ten thousand talents of silver could not be considered as a compensation to the state for the loss of a whole nation of people throughout all their generations.
entries.033a9562d91f8dda668a52a5b2dbae530df74f67: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen15583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15584" type="x-p"/> Who is he, and where is he - There is a wonderful abruptness and confusion in the original words, highly expressive of the state of mind in which the king then was: מי הוא זה ואי זה הוא אשר מלאו לבו לעשות כן mi hu zeh veey zeh hu asher melao libbo laasoth ken. "Who? He? This one? And where? This one? He? Who hath filled his heart to do thus?" He was at once struck with the horrible nature of a conspiracy so cruel and diabolic.
entries.937c894a43143c5b057c2b8ce613a37df1d65847: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen15584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15585" type="x-p"/> Haman stood up - He rose from the table to make request for his life, as soon as the king had gone out; and then he fell on his knees before the queen, she still sitting upon her couch.
entries.6b42d02d70e1e77f972f3a8810b547e85c3d023c: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen15585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15586" type="x-p"/> Will he force the queen - On the king's return he found him at the queen's knees; and, professing to think that he intended to do violence to her honor, used the above expressions; though he must have known that, in such circumstances, the thought of perpetrating an act of this kind could not possibly exist. <div eID="gen15586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15587" type="x-p"/> They covered Haman's face - This was a sign of his being devoted to death: for the attendants saw that the king was determined on his destruction. When a criminal was condemned by a Roman judge, he was delivered into the hands of the serjeant with these words: I, lictor; caput obnubito, arbori infelici suspendito. "Go, serjeant; cover his head, and hang him on the accursed tree."
entries.05563398cf3c51c0eecbf95411e1cea4b6be4817: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen15587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15588" type="x-p"/> Behold also, the gallows - As if he had said, Besides all he has determined to do to the Jews, he has erected a very high gallows, on which he had determined, this very day, to hang Mordecai, who has saved the king's life. <div eID="gen15588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15589" type="x-p"/> Hang him thereon - Let him be instantly impaled on the same post. "Harm watch, harm catch," says the proverb. Perillus was the first person burnt alive in the brazen bull which he had made for the punishment of others; hence the poet said: - - Nec lex est justior ulla, Quam necis artifices arte perire sua. "Nor can there be a juster law than that the artificers of death should perish by their own invention."  <chapter eID="Esth.7"/> <div eID="gen15589" type="x-p"/>

entries.49dd5ee4898e1ba0d96840719406638402a4b8dd: <reference osisRef="Esth.7.1">Est 7:1</reference> <div eID="gen6775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6776" type="x-p"/> The king and Haman came to drink (לשׁתּות), i.e., to partake of the משׁתּה, in the queen’s apartment.
entries.2ae0c40fcda3f76cd3143c98015f1766e14f5797: <reference osisRef="Esth.7.2-Esth.7.4">Est 7:2-4</reference> <div eID="gen6776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6777" type="x-p"/> At this banquet of wine the king asked again on the second day, as he had done on the first (<reference osisRef="Esth.5.6">Est 5:6</reference>): What is thy petition, Queen Esther, etc.? Esther then took courage to express her petition. After the usual introductory phrases (<reference osisRef="Esth.7.3">Est 7:3</reference> like <reference osisRef="Esth.5.8">Est 5:8</reference>), she replied: “Let my life be given me at my petition, and my people at my request.” For, she adds as a justification and reason for such a petition, “we are sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be slain, and to perish. And if we had been sold for bondmen and bondwomen, I had been silent, for the enemy is not worth the king’s damage.” In this request עמּי is a short expression for: the life of my people, and the preposition ב, the so-called בּ <hi type="italic">pretii</hi>. The request is conceived of as the price which she offers or presents for her life and that of her people. The expression נמכּרנוּ, we are sold, is used by Esther with reference to the offer of Haman to pay a large sum into the royal treasury for the extermination of the Jews, <reference osisRef="Esth.3.9">Est 3:9</reference>; Est 4:7. אלּוּ, contracted after Aramaean usage from לוּ אם, and occurring also <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.6">Ecc 6:6</reference>, supposes a case, the realization of which is desired, but not to be expected, the matter being represented as already decided by the use of the perfect. The last clause, וגו הצּר אין כּי, is by most expositors understood as a reference, on the part of Esther, to the financial loss which the king would incur by the extermination of the Jews. Thus Rambach, e.g., following R. Sal. ben Melech, understands the meaning expressed to be<hi type="italic">: hostis nullo modo aequare, compensare, resarcire potest pecunia sua damnum, quod rex ex nostro excidio patitur.</hi> So also Cler. and others. The confirmatory clause would in this case refer not to החרשׁתּי, but to a negative notion needing completion: but I dare not be silent; and such completion is itself open to objection. To this must be added, that שׁוה in Kal constructed with בּ does not signify <hi type="italic">compensare</hi>, to equalize, to make equal, but to be equal; consequently the Piel should be found here to justify the explanation proposed. שׁוה in Kal constructed with בּ signifies to be of equal worth with something, to equal another thing in value. Hence Gesenius translates: the enemy does not equal the damage of the king, i.e., is not in a condition to compensate the damage. But neither when thus viewed does the sentence give any reason for Esther’s statement, that she would have been silent, if the Jews had been sold for salves. Hence we are constrained, with Bertheau, to take a different view of the words, and to give up the reference to financial loss. נזק, in the Targums, means not merely financial, but also bodily, personal damage; e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.91.7">Psa 91:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.26.11">Gen 26:11</reference>, to do harm, 1Ch 16:22. Hence the phrase may be understood thus: For the enemy is not equal to, is not worth, the damage of the king, i.e., not worthy that I should annoy the king with my petition. Thus Esther says, <reference osisRef="Esth.7.4">Est 7:4</reference> : The enemy has determined upon the total destruction of my people. If he only intended to bring upon them grievous oppression, even that most grievous oppression of slavery, I would have been silent, for the enemy is not worthy that I should vex or annoy the king by my accusation.
entries.81ca1614cada8cea109b8bdca6b80cd85e16963c: <reference osisRef="Esth.7.5">Est 7:5</reference> <div eID="gen6777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6778" type="x-p"/> The king, whose indignation was excited by what he had just heard, asks with an agitation, shown by the repetition of the ויּאמר: “Who is he, and where is he, whose heart hath filled him (whom his heart hath filled) to do so?” Evil thoughts proceed from the heart, and fill the man, and impel him to evil deeds: <reference osisRef="Isa.44.20">Isa 44:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.11">Ecc 8:11</reference>; Mat 15:19.
entries.a76f569ae5ba56d22c4360b720e87c596df4749a: <reference osisRef="Esth.7.6">Est 7:6</reference> <div eID="gen6778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6779" type="x-p"/> Esther replies: “The adversary and enemy is this wicked Haman.” Then was Haman afraid before the king and the queen. נבעת as in <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.30">1Ch 21:30</reference>; Dan 8:17.
entries.6dbfc5eb4003d958f0141445ada036d5091f7a60: <reference osisRef="Esth.7.7">Est 7:7</reference> <div eID="gen6779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6780" type="x-p"/> The king in his wrath arose from the banquet of wine, and went into the garden of the house (קם is here a pregnant expression, and is also combined with אל־גּנּת); but Haman remained standing to beg for his life to Queen Esther (על בּקּשׁ as in <reference osisRef="Esth.4.8">Est 4:8</reference>), “for he saw that there was evil determined against him by the king” (כּלה, completed, i.e., determined; comp. <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.7">1Sa 20:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.9">1Sa 20:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.17">1Sa 25:17</reference>, and elsewhere); and hence that he had no mercy to expect from him, unless the queen should intercede for him.
entries.01f7dbfd93f47c9732b220ddc50aaeccf34dc855: <reference osisRef="Esth.7.8">Est 7:8</reference> <div eID="gen6780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6781" type="x-p"/> The king returned to the house, and found Haman falling (נפל as in <reference osisRef="Josh.8.10">Jos 8:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.21.1">Deu 21:1</reference>, and elsewhere) at or on the couch on which Esther was (sitting), i.e., falling as a suppliant at her feet; and crediting Haman in the heat of his anger with the worst designs, he cried out: “Shall also violence be done to the queen before me in the house?” The <hi type="italic">infin</hi>. לכבּושׁ after the interrogatory particle signifies: Is violence to be done, i.e., shall violence be done? as in <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.2">1Ch 15:2</reference> and elsewhere; comp. Ewald, §237, <hi type="italic">c</hi>. כּבשׁ, to tread under foot, to subdue, used here in the more general sense, to offer violence. Without waiting for an explanation, the king, still more infuriated, passes sentence of death upon Haman. This is not given in so many words by the historian, but we are told immediately that: “as the word went out of the king’s mouth, they covered Haman’s face.” הדּבר is not the speech of the king just reported, but the judicial sentence, the death warrant, i.e., the word to punish Haman with death. This is unmistakeably shown by the further statement: they covered Haman’s face. The subject is indefinite: the attendants present. To cover the face was indeed to begin to carry the sentence of death into execution. With respect to this custom, expositors appeal to Curtius, vi. 8. 22: <hi type="italic">Philetam</hi> - <hi type="italic">capite velato in regiam adducunt;</hi> and Cicero, <hi type="italic">pro C. Rabirio iv. 13: I lictor, colliga manus, caput obnubito, arbori infelici suspendito.</hi>
entries.45d246850575545f423339e5878981ee11d39aaf: <reference osisRef="Esth.7.9-Esth.7.10">Est 7:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen6781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6782" type="x-p"/> Then said Harbonah (already mentioned <reference osisRef="Esth.1.10">Est 1:10</reference>), one of the eunuchs before the king, i.e., who held office before the king: “Behold also the tree which Haman made (comp. <reference osisRef="Esth.5.14">Est 5:14</reference>) stands in the house of Haman.” גּם points to the fact that the other eunuchs had already brought forward various particulars concerning Haman’s crime. Mordochai, who had spoken good for the king, viz., when he gave information of the conspiracy, <reference osisRef="Esth.2.22">Est 2:22</reference>; Est 6:2. On this tree the king ordered that Haman should be hanged, and this sentence was executed without delay. - “And the king’s wrath was pacified.” With this remark the narrative of this occurrence is closed, and the history pursues its further course as follows. Mordochai Advanced to Haman’s Position. Counter-Edict for the Preservation of Jews - Esther 8 <div eID="gen6782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6783" type="x-p"/> The king bestowed the house of Haman on Esther, and advanced Mordochai to Haman’s place of prime minister (vv. 1 and 2). Esther then earnestly besought the king for the abolition of the edict published by Haman against the Jews, and the king permitted her and Mordochai to send letters in the king’s name to all the Jews in his kingdom, commanding them to stand for their life, and to slay their enemies, on the day appointed for their own extermination (<reference osisRef="Esth.8.3-Esth.8.14">Est 8:3-14</reference>). These measures diffused great joy throughout the kingdom (<reference osisRef="Esth.8.15-Esth.8.17">Est 8:15-17</reference>).  <chapter eID="Esth.7"/> <div eID="gen6783" type="x-p"/>

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="7" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. VII.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 SO the king and Haman came <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>to drink.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> to banquet with Esther the queen.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And the king said again to Esther, on the se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cond day, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 5. 6.</ns0:note> at the banquet of wine <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">So it is called to note that it was not designed for a seast to fill their bellies, but rather for a banquet to delight and please their palates with wine and other delicacies, see on <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 5. 8.</ns0:note>, What <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> thy petition, queen Esther? and it shall be grant<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed thee: and what <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> thy request? and it shall be performed, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> to the half of the king<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 Then Esther the queen answered and said, If I have found favour in thy sight, O king, and if it please the king, let my life be given me at my pe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tition <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">It is my humble and only request that thou wouldst not give me up to the malice of that man that <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>esigns to take away my life, and will certainly do it, if thou dost not prevent it.</ns0:note>, and my people <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>And</ns0:hi> the lives (which is easily supplied out of the foregoing branch) <ns0:hi>of my people</ns0:hi> the Jews, of whom I am descended.</ns0:note> at my request.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 For we are <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 3. 9.</ns0:note> sold <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">By the craft and cruelty of that man who offered a great sum of mony to purchase our destruction.</ns0:note>, I and my people <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">For we are all given up to his malice and rage, without any exception of my own person.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>that they should de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stroy, and kill, and cause to pe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rish.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> to be destroyed, to be slain, and to perish <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">She useth variety of expressions to make the deeper impression upon the Kings mind.</ns0:note>: but if we had been sold for bond-men, and bond-women, I had held my tongue <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Because that calamity had neither been irrecoverable, nor intolerable, nor yet unprofitable to the King for whose honour and service, I should willingly have submitted my self and people to any kind of bondage.</ns0:note>, al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />though the enemy could not countervail the kings damage <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">His ten thousand ta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lents, if paid into the Kings treasury, would not repair the Kings loss in the customs and tributes which the King receives from the Jews within his dominions.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 Then the king Ahasuerus answered and said unto Esther the queen, Who <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> he? and where <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> he <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">The expressions are short and doubled, as proceeding from a discomposed and enraged mind.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>w<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>se heart <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> 
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>
                           <ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led him.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> that durst presume in his heart to do so <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> To circumvent me, and by subtilty to procure an irrevocable decree, whereby not only my estate should be so much impaired, and so many of my innocent Subjects be destroyed without mercy, but my Queen also should be involved in the same danger and destruction.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And Esther said, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> adversary.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> The adversary and enemy <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Of the King, and of my Person and People.</ns0:note> this wicked Haman. Then Haman was afraid, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>at the presence of.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> before the king and the queen.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And the king arising from the banquet of wine in his wrath, <ns0:hi>went</ns0:hi> into the palace-garden <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Partly as disdaining the company and sight of so ungrateful and audacious a person: partly to cool and allay his troubled and inflamed spirits, and partly to consider within himself the hainous<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness of <ns0:hi>Hamans</ns0:hi> crime, and the mischief which himself had done by his own rashness. and what punishment was fit to be inflicted upon so great a delinquent.</ns0:note>: and Haman stood up to make request for his life to Esther the queen: for he saw <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">By the violent commotion of the Kings mind and passions.</ns0:note> that there was evil determined against him by the king.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 Then the king returned out of the palace-gar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />den, into the place of the banquet of wine, and Haman was fallen upon the bed <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>by,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>beside the bed,</ns0:hi> on which the Queen sat at meat, after the manner: where he was fallen upon his knees, and upon the ground, at her feet, as humble suppliants used to do, and as the Queen did at the Kings feet, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 8. 3.</ns0:note> whereon Esther <ns0:hi>was.</ns0:hi> Then said the king, Will he force the queen also <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Will he now attempt my Queens Chastity as he hath already attempted her life! His pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sumption and impudence I see will stick at nothing. He speaks not this out of a real jealousy, for which there was no cause in those circumstances, but from an exasperated mind which takes all occa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sions to vent itself against the person who gave the provocation, and makes the worst construction of all his words and action.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> 
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> before me in the house <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">In my own presence and palace.</ns0:note>? As the word went out of the kings mouth they <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The Kings and Queens Chamberlains then attending upon them.</ns0:note> covered Ha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mans face <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Partly that the King might not be offended or grieved with the sight of a Person whom he now loathed: and partly because they looked upon him as a condemned person; for the faces of such used to be covered.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 1. 10.</ns0:note> Harbonah, one of the chamberlains <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Who knew this either by his own observation, or by the in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />formation of some of his brethren, who were lately sent to <ns0:hi>Hamans</ns0:hi> house, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 6. 14. where they might easily see it, or at least hear of it. And this he said, either out of a distast which he had taken against <ns0:hi>Haman</ns0:hi> for his great insolency, and barbarous cruelty: or in com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pliance with the Kings inclinations, and the Queens desires.</ns0:note>, said before the king, Behold also the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> gallows fifty cubits high, which Haman had made for Mor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />decai, who had spoken good for the king <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven to the saving of the Kings life, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 2. 21, 22, 23. and therefore deserved a better requital than this even from <ns0:hi>Haman,</ns0:hi> if he had not basely preferred the satisfaction of his own revenge before the preservation of the Kings life.</ns0:note>, stand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth in the house of Haman. Then the king said, Hang him thereon.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Which stood in his own house, as was now said, and made the punishment more grievous and ignominious.</ns0:note> for Mordecai. Then was the kings wrath pacified <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Judgment being now most justly executed upon this abominable criminal.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
